sections.h2: What is probate called in Louisiana, and where does it happen?
sections.html:
Louisiana calls the process a succession, and the goal is a judgment of possession or an affidavit that shows who now owns the estate. Venue follows the decedent's domicile at death, so the petition goes to the district court for that parish. In Orleans Parish the Civil District Court handles it, according to the Loyola pro bono desk manual.

If the decedent lived outside Louisiana, the succession can be opened in any parish where the person owned immovable property. A seller dealing with an inherited house should first confirm which parish court, or which clerk of court, holds the file.

sections.h2: What is a small succession and what is the dollar limit now?
sections.html:
A small succession is one where the gross value of the estate is $200,000 or less at the date of death, if the decedent was domiciled in Louisiana. That limit is stated in Code of Civil Procedure art. 3421, which also sets a second tier for ancillary successions.

Type of small successionLimit in art. 3421
Decedent domiciled in LouisianaGross value of $200,000 or less at date of death
Decedent domiciled elsewhere, Louisiana property only (ancillary)Gross value of $125,000 or less at date of death
Death at least 20 years before the affidavit is signedNo dollar limit

Older guides, including some law school and title materials, still describe $125,000 as the general cap. The legislature's current article text reads $200,000 for domiciled decedents, so check the date on anything you read.

sections.h2: Who can use the affidavit instead of going to court?
sections.html:
Article 3431 says it is not necessary to open a small succession judicially in three situations. All of them are narrower than they sound, so read the list closely.

  • A Louisiana domiciliary who died without a will.
  • A Louisiana domiciliary who died with a will but left no immovable property in the state, and only if the surviving spouse and every person who would inherit with or without the will agree to waive probate.
  • A non-domiciliary who died without a will, or whose will was probated by court order in another state.

A decedent with a will who owned a house in Louisiana does not fit the second item, because the house is immovable property. That estate needs a judicial route. Paragraph B of the same article also lets a governor-appointed public administrator use the affidavit for small estates with no heir present, after a single advertisement in the official parish journal and no notice of opposition.

sections.h2: What goes in the small succession affidavit?
sections.html:
Article 3432 covers the intestate affidavit, and it must be sworn by at least two people. When there is a surviving spouse, the spouse signs along with one or more heirs. With no spouse, at least two heirs sign, or one heir and a second person with actual knowledge of the facts if there is only one heir.

  • The date of death, domicile, marital status and last residence of the decedent.
  • Each heir's name, last known address and relationship, and why any non-signing heir did not sign: unlocatable after reasonable diligence, or given 30 days' notice by mail without objecting.
  • A description of the property, labeled community or separate, with enough detail for an immovable to be transferred.
  • The value of each item and the total at death, plus each heir's interest and any usufruct of the surviving spouse.
  • A statement that each signing heir accepts the succession, sworn under penalty of perjury.

Article 3433, added by Acts 2024, No. 90, covers a non-domiciliary who died with a will. It also requires a copy of the will and a certified copy of the other state's probate order, and a legatee's acceptance.

sections.h2: How does the affidavit move title to a house?
sections.html:
The affidavit, or a certified copy, has to be recorded in the conveyance records of the parish where the immovable is located. Article 3434 says a recorded affidavit is admissible and is prima facie evidence of the facts it states, including the heirs' relationship to the decedent and their rights in the property.

The same article lets banks and others holding money or property rely on a multiple original or certified copy as authority to pay or deliver to the named successors, and it discharges them when they do.

There is a catch for anyone left out of the affidavit. A person who claims to be a successor but is not named has two years from the recording date to assert an interest against a third party who acquired the property for value, or that party's successors. Civil Code art. 3338 and R.S. 9:2721 explain why recording in the correct parish matters: an unrecorded instrument has no effect on third persons, and the recorded conveyance must name who pays property tax and give a mailing address for tax notices.

sections.h2: When is a court-run succession needed, and how does it work?
sections.html:
You need a judicial succession when the facts fall outside the affidavit rules, such as a will that has to be probated, a house in a testate estate, or an estate above the dollar limit. The aim is a judgment of possession that recognizes the heirs or legatees and places them in possession.

For an intestate estate that is relatively free from debt, Code of Civil Procedure arts. 3001 through 3008 allow an ex parte petition for possession by all competent heirs who accept the succession. The desk manual says the petition usually comes with an Affidavit of Death, Domicile and Heirship under arts. 2821 and 2822, signed by two people with knowledge. Civil Code art. 962 presumes that a successor accepts unless there is a written renunciation, which is why filings usually include every successor.

For a testate estate, art. 3031 lets a court put legatees in possession on an ex parte petition from all general and universal legatees, provided the will has been probated, each legatee is competent or represented and accepts, and no creditor has demanded administration. The desk manual adds that a will must be probated within five years of the judicial opening of the succession, under art. 2893, and that a succession representative named in the will has to join the petition for possession.

sections.h2: Can a succession representative sell the house?
sections.html:
Yes, by private sale if the court approves it. Under Code of Civil Procedure art. 3281, the representative files a petition describing the property, the price and conditions, and the reasons for selling privately, and attaches any sale agreement already signed.

The representative may sign the agreement first, but it is subject to the suspensive condition that the court approve the sale. The petition is due within 30 days after the agreement is signed.

This timeline matters for heirs who are in a hurry. A buyer can sign a contract while the court paperwork runs, and the closing then waits on the approval.

sections.h2: What does a Louisiana heir face when selling an inherited house?
sections.html:
The common problems are proving who owns the house and paying carrying costs while the paperwork runs.

  • Surviving spouse protections: homestead rights under R.S. 20:1 reach the surviving spouse and minor children of a deceased owner, and the constitutional homestead exemption can continue for a surviving spouse who occupies the home.
  • Property taxes: the tax is a charge on the land, so unpaid balances travel with the house. Redemption after a tax sale costs the taxes, a 5 percent penalty and 1 percent simple interest per month, per the desk manual's chapter on real estate taxes.
  • Storm and flood damage: Louisiana's gulf location and hurricane history, noted in the state overview, can add repair and insurance questions.

A cash buyer will still need the heirs' ownership documents to close. Sorting out the affidavit or judgment first can shorten the process, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is can take over the repair worries that stall many inherited sales.

faqs.q: Do I have to go through court to inherit a house in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Not always. If the decedent lived in Louisiana, died without a will, and the estate is $200,000 or less, a small succession affidavit under arts. 3431 and 3432 can work. A will plus a house usually means a judicial succession.

faqs.q: How much is a small succession in Louisiana?
faqs.a: $200,000 or less in gross value for a Louisiana domiciliary, and $125,000 or less for an ancillary succession of someone domiciled elsewhere. A death at least 20 years before the affidavit has no dollar limit under art. 3421.

faqs.q: Who signs a small succession affidavit?
faqs.a: At least two people. If there is a surviving spouse, the spouse signs plus at least one heir. With no spouse, two heirs sign, or one heir and another person with actual knowledge of the facts.
In the conveyance records of the parish where the house is located, under art. 3434. Banks and other holders of the decedent's money may also rely on a certified copy to pay the named heirs.

faqs.q: Can I sell the house before the succession is finished?
faqs.a: A succession representative can sign a private sale agreement before court approval, but the contract is subject to a suspensive condition that the court approve it. The petition must be filed within 30 days of signing.
